read.sections.0.text.source: New technology raises questions about who it helps, who it might harm and who decides. A government or parliament makes laws, which everyone must follow, and courts can act when a law is broken. Companies write rules for their own tools. Groups of countries can agree on a guideline, which is advice that each country can choose to use. In 2021, all 193 member states of UNESCO adopted one for AI. Residents, including young people, can take part too, by sharing their views when leaders ask. In the made-up town of Hillford, the council holds a meeting before it uses AI. Students, an older neighbour and a newer resident who can't vote yet all speak.
read.sections.0.text.back: New technology raises questions about who it helps, who it might harm, and who decides. A government or parliament makes laws, which everyone must follow, and courts can act when a law is broken. Companies write rules for their own tools. Groups of countries can agree on a guideline, which is advice each country may choose to use. In 2021, all 193 member states of UNESCO adopted one guideline for AI. Residents, including young people, can also take part, by sharing their views when leaders ask. In the made-up town of Hillford, the town council holds a meeting before using AI. Students, an older neighbour, and a new resident who can't vote yet all speak.

read.sections.1.heading.source: Two regional choices: a guide and a law
read.sections.1.heading.back: Two regions' choices: a guide and a law

read.sections.1.text.source: In February 2024, the digital ministers of ASEAN, a group of Southeast Asian countries, shared the ASEAN Guide on AI Governance and Ethics. It sets out seven ideas, such as fairness, privacy, safety and putting people first. It is voluntary, and each country keeps its own laws. It also notes that its members are at different stages with digital technology. The European Union (EU) chose a law. Its AI Act came into force in August 2024, with parts starting on different dates. It sorts uses of AI by risk. Risk means how much harm they could do. Since February 2025, some uses are banned, such as scores that treat people unfairly. Since August 2026, a chatbot must make clear that it is a machine. Strict checks for high-risk uses, such as marking exams, start in December 2027. Most uses, like spam filters, have no special AI rules, but other laws, like privacy laws, still apply.
read.sections.1.text.back: In February 2024, the digital ministers of ASEAN, a group of Southeast Asian countries, shared the ASEAN Guide on AI Governance and Ethics. The guide sets out seven ideas, such as fairness, privacy, safety and putting people first. The guide is voluntary, and each country keeps using its own laws. The guide also notes that its member countries are at different stages with digital technology. The European Union (EU) chose a law. The EU's AI Act came into force in August 2024, with parts starting on different dates. The law sorts uses of AI by their risk. Risk means how much harm they could cause. Since February 2025, some uses are banned, such as scores that treat people unfairly. Since August 2026, a chatbot must make clear that it is a machine. Strict checks for high-risk uses, such as marking exams, start in December 2027. Most uses, such as spam filters, have no special AI rules, but other laws, such as privacy laws, still apply.

read.sections.2.heading.source: Rules for useful AI, and your own view
read.sections.2.heading.back: Rules for useful AI, and your own view

read.sections.2.text.source: Rules are not only about stopping harm. The ASEAN guide says one of its aims is to build trust, so that people and groups can use AI with care. In Thailand, Traffy Fondue, a public service built by a national science agency, uses AI to sort residents' reports about problems such as floods. It sends each report to the right office, where people decide what to do. Rules about privacy, and about who checks the AI's work, are meant to help people trust tools like this. Keep two questions apart. “What does the EU law say about marking exams?” has a factual answer. “What should Hillford do?” asks for your recommendation, and yours can be different from any law, if you give reasons.

The service sends each report to the right office, where people decide what to do. Rules about privacy, and about who checks the AI's work, are meant to help people trust tools like this. Keep two questions apart. “What does the EU law say about marking exams?” has a factual answer. “What should Hillford do?” asks for your recommendation, and your recommendation may differ from any law, as long as you give reasons.

watch.summary.source: This video is from UNESCO. UNESCO is a world group that works on schools, science and culture. The video is part of a series about the ethics of AI. Ethics means what is right and wrong. The video asks a big question. How can people get the good things from AI without making gaps between people bigger? AI could also bring new kinds of unfair results. The video says people around the world seem to agree on some ideas. These include privacy, equal treatment and leaving no one out. The hard part is turning these ideas into real rules. The video looks at how different parts of the world are making rules for AI. It also asks what would make rules fair for everyone, everywhere.

educatorNotes.0.source: Keep two questions apart: “What do you recommend for Hillford?” (the learner's view, marked on reasons) and “What does the European Union's law say?” (a fact about one jurisdiction). Never mark a recommendation wrong because it differs from the EU law. The AI Act (in force 1 August 2024) bans, from 2 February 2025, social scoring that leads to unjustified or unrelated harmful treatment, emotion recognition in workplaces and schools except for medical or safety reasons, and live face identification by police in public places except for three narrow purposes (searching for victims or missing persons, preventing an imminent threat, and finding suspects of serious crimes). Transparency rules (chatbots, labelled deepfakes) apply from 2 August 2026. After the Digital Omnibus on AI, high-risk rules for uses such as exam scoring (Annex III) apply from 2 December 2027, and for AI in regulated products (Annex I) from 2 August 2028 (the Commission's AI Act Service Desk timeline, read 8 November 2026); check it before quoting dates. Minimal-risk uses (spam filters, games) have no AI Act rules, but data protection, consumer protection and product safety law still apply (Article 2). The shop owner's market camera: live identification by police is what the Act bans; a shop's or council's own cameras fall under other rules, such as data protection.

Minimal-risk uses (spam filters, games) have no AI Act rules, but data protection, consumer protection and product safety law still apply (Article 2). educatorNotes.1.source: The ASEAN Guide on AI Governance and Ethics was unveiled at the 4th ASEAN Digital Ministers' Meeting on 2 February 2024. It says adoption is voluntary and that it doesn't override national or sector laws, and calls itself a living document. Its seven principles are transparency and explainability, fairness and equity, security and safety, human-centricity, privacy and data governance, accountability and integrity, and robustness and reliability. It recommends national steps (training people, supporting new companies and research, raising public awareness, tools that help businesses follow the guide) and regional ones (an ASEAN working group on AI governance, adapting the guide for generative AI, a collection of use cases), and asks organisations to consider “the differing levels of digital maturity across ASEAN”. Traffy Fondue (Thailand) was developed by NECTEC, part of NSTDA; its AI classifies residents' reports and sends each to the responsible agency, and people decide and act. NSTDA reports more than 940,000 reports from June 2022 to July 2024, its own figures. Lesson 10 may teach it in more depth.
educatorNotes.1.back: The ASEAN Guide on AI Governance and Ethics was launched at the 4th ASEAN Digital Ministers' Meeting on 2 February 2024. The guide says its adoption is voluntary and does not override national or sector laws, and calls itself a living document (one that keeps being updated). Its seven principles are transparency and explainability, fairness and equity, security and safety, human-centricity, privacy and data governance, accountability and integrity, and robustness and reliability. The guide recommends national steps (training people, supporting new companies and research, raising public awareness, tools that help businesses follow the guide) and regional steps (an ASEAN working group on AI governance, adapting the guide for generative AI, a collection of use cases), and asks organisations to consider “the differing levels of digital maturity across ASEAN” (gloss in brackets). Traffy Fondue (Thailand) was developed by NECTEC, part of NSTDA; its AI classifies residents' reports and sends each to the responsible agency, then people decide and act. NSTDA reports more than 940,000 reports from June 2022 to July 2024, by its own figures. Lesson 10 may cover it in more depth.
educatorNotes.1.note: The principles' Indonesian names are this draft's own; the guide has no official Indonesian version that the drafter could check.

educatorNotes.2.source: To localise: Indonesia's Minister of Communication and Informatics issued a circular on AI ethics (Surat Edaran No. 9 of 2023), and Malaysia launched voluntary national guidelines in 2024 (links in the claim record, content/courses/digital-world/claims/DW16.md). Like the UNESCO and ASEAN texts, both are guidance rather than laws. Present every approach neutrally: the lesson compares choices, it doesn't rank countries or regions. Like the UNESCO and ASEAN texts, both are guidance, not laws. Present every approach neutrally: the lesson compares choices, it does not rank countries or regions.
